tip: Valoir le coup is literally 'to be worth the blow' – the everyday way to say something's worth it. Ça vaudrait le coup = it'd be worth it.
For time still to come, dans means 'in', not 'within': dans cinq minutes = five minutes from now, not sometime in the next five.
French weather runs on faire (to make): il fera très chaud is literally 'it will make very hot'. Same for cold and wind – il fera froid.
French drops the 'on' before weekdays: lundi alone means 'on Monday'. Add le – le lundi – and it flips to 'on Mondays', every week.
Where English says 'when I'm done', French looks ahead: quand j'aurai terminé is literally 'when I will have finished'. Future stacks on future.
Never put a conditional after si. The 'would' verb sits in the other clause: si j'avais (had), je voyagerais (would travel).
Plaire flips the subject: ça me plairait is literally 'it would please me', not 'I would like it'. The thing you enjoy does the pleasing.
N'avoir qu'à means 'to only have to', i.e. just: tu n'auras qu'à me passer un coup de fil = you'll just have to give me a call.
Clothes 'go' on you in French: te va très bien means 'suits you', from aller (to go). Ça te va = it looks good on you.
An event doesn't 'happen', it 'has place': avoir lieu = to take place. La réunion aura lieu = the meeting will take place.
Countries carry an article in French: le Japon, not just 'Japan'. You visit le Japon, la France, les États-Unis.
France runs on the 24-hour clock: vingt heures is 8 PM, not 20 in the morning. Subtract 12 to get the evening time.
Drop the article before a profession: je deviendrais artiste, not 'un artiste'. French names the job bare – il est médecin.
